t: Vibe Manager is an open-source, self-hosted platform on which an enterprise's employees and their AI coding agents build, deploy and run internal applications against shared, IT-governed infrastructure. The latest release, v0.1.3 , is still a minimal one, to try it. It is not for untrusted Applications or real company data : its release notes say what works and what is missing.

There are two people in these documents. They can be the same person. The Platform administrator installs the platform on a server and connects it to the company's sign-in (OIDC). The Builder installs the tool vibe on their own computer, makes an Application, tries it there, deploys it and shares it. Getting started takes both from nothing to an Application open in a browser, in one page.

Installing with Compose : the files, the values, the certificate, the first start and the setup credential. Connecting OIDC : registering the platform at the identity provider, vibe admin connect-oidc , signing in, and when a sign-in fails. TLS : the Compose file's reverse proxy, your own reverse proxy, or the program serving TLS itself. Your own Postgres : a Postgres 18 of your own instead of the bundled one. Upgrading and stopping , and how the containers are hardened.

Making it and running it locally : vibe new , vibe check , vibe dev , vibe request . Deploying : vibe deploy , and the Versions it makes. Sharing : vibe share , and the Dashboard. The tool's commands : every command, as its --help prints it. The SDK's types : what an Application is written with. The words these pages use (Application, Resource, Grant, Version, Contributor, ...) are defined in the Glossary .

This page takes you from nothing to an Application open in your browser. It uses the files of the release v0.1.3 only. Read the release's notes first: this release is not for untrusted Applications or real company data. There are two people in this page. They can be the same person. The administrator installs the platform on a server and connects it to the company's sign-in (OIDC). The Builder installs the tool vibe on their own computer, makes an Application, tries it there, deploys it and shares it. Every command below uses the domain vibe.example.com . Put your own domain in its place.

For the installation: a Linux server with Docker Engine 25.0 or later and its Compose plugin 2.24.1 or later, on x86-64 (the image is for linux/amd64 only). That minimum is read from Docker's notes and was not tried; deploy/README.md names the versions the install tests ran with; a domain whose names all reach the server: a DNS record for *.vibe.example.com . Applications are at <name>.vibe.example.com ; a certificate for *.vibe.example.com and its private key, in PEM; an OIDC identity provider at which you can register a client. For the Builder's computer: Linux on x86-64 with glibc 2.35 or later (Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12 and later), or macOS on Apple silicon; Node.js 22 or later, with npm ; git .

On the server, make a folder and download the release's files into it: sh mkdir -p /opt/vibe/certs /opt/vibe/ca cd /opt/vibe curl -fLO https://github.com/Irvingouj/vm-manager/releases/download/v0.1.3/compose.yaml curl -fLO https://github.com/Irvingouj/vm-manager/releases/download/v0.1.3/env.example curl -fLO https://github.com/Irvingouj/vm-manager/releases/download/v0.1.3/SHA256SUMS sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS The last command checks the files you downloaded. Each line must end with OK . Make the file of values, .env , from env.example . Three values are required: the domain, the installation's key and the password of the bundled Postgres. sh cp env.example .env chmod 600 .env sed -i "s|^VIBE_DOMAIN=.*|VIBE_DOMAIN=vibe.example.com|" .env sed -i "s|^VIBE_SECRET_KEY=.*|VIBE_SECRET_KEY=$(openssl rand -base64 32)|" .env sed -i "s|^POSTGRES_PASSWORD=.*|POSTGRES_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 24)|" .env Without the domain or the key, docker compose refuses to start and names the value. Without the password, the bundled Postgres does not start and docker compose logs postgres names POSTGRES_PASSWORD : set it and run docker compose up -d again. Keep .env as long as you keep

h: 2. Register the platform at your identity provider
t: At your identity provider, register an OpenID Connect client for the platform, with a client secret and the authorization code flow: the redirect address is https://auth.vibe.example.com/callback ; the scopes are openid profile email offline_access . The provider must allow offline_access for this client and for every person who signs in; the ID token holds the person's Groups in the claim groups ; the ID token is signed with RS256 or ES256 . Note the issuer, the client id and the client secret. Choose the Group whose members are Platform administrators. Then, on the server, print the setup credential. It is shown once, and it is good for 24 hours: sh docker compose exec vibe vibe setup

On each computer that uses the tool: the administrator's for the next step, and each Builder's. On Linux ( x86-64 ): sh curl -fLO https://github.com/Irvingouj/vm-manager/releases/download/v0.1.3/vibe-0.1.3-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz curl -fLO https://github.com/Irvingouj/vm-manager/releases/download/v0.1.3/SHA256SUMS sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS tar -xzf vibe-0.1.3-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz mkdir -p ~/.local/bin cp vibe-0.1.3-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/vibe ~/.local/bin/vibe On macOS (Apple silicon): sh curl -fLO https://github.com/Irvingouj/vm-manager/releases/download/v0.1.3/vibe-0.1.3-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz curl -fLO https://github.com/Irvingouj/vm-manager/releases/download/v0.1.3/SHA256SUMS shasum -a 256 --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS tar -xzf vibe-0.1.3-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz mkdir -p ~/.local/bin cp vibe-0.1.3-aarch64-apple-darwin/vibe ~/.local/bin/vibe The macOS program is not signed by a developer and not notarised by Apple. Downloaded with curl , as above, it runs. If you downloaded the archive with a browser, macOS holds the program back. Remove its quarantine mark: sh xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ~/.local/bin/vibe ~/.local/bin mu

The administrator connects the identity provider with the tool, from any computer that reaches the installation over HTTPS. The two read lines ask for the setup credential and the client secret without showing them: sh read -rs VIBE_SETUP_CREDENTIAL && export VIBE_SETUP_CREDENTIAL read -rs VIBE_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET && export VIBE_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET vibe admin connect-oidc --domain vibe.example.com \ --issuer https://idp.example.com \ --client-id vibe \ --administrators-group vibe-administrators Now curl https://api.vibe.example.com/v1/installation says "sign_in":"oidc" .

The Builder signs the tool in. It opens the browser at the company's sign-in, and comes back signed in: sh vibe sign-in --domain vibe.example.com vibe whoami On a computer without a browser, add --no-browser : the tool shows an address to open on another device.

Make a project from the template, install its packages, and check it: sh vibe new hello cd hello npm install vibe check hello is the Application's name. It becomes its address: https://hello.vibe.example.com/ . The project's AGENTS.md tells you and your coding agent how to work in it.

sh vibe dev Open http://hello.localhost:7480/ in your browser. You choose there which test User you are; the test Users are in vibe.dev.json . The project is built again each time you change it. Stop it with Ctrl+C . The first run downloads Postgres 18 once, for the Application's own database on your computer. You can also send one request without a browser: sh vibe request --as outsider /

A deploy sends the project's last commit, so the project must be a Git repository with everything committed: sh git init git add --all git commit -m "The first version" vibe deploy The Application now answers at https://hello.vibe.example.com/ . Open it in your browser: you are its Contributor, so you can open it.

Let others open it. Share it with a person by their email address (they must have signed in to the installation once), with a Group, or with everyone who can sign in: sh vibe share hello --email colleague@example.com vibe share hello --group engineering vibe share hello --everyone

vibe --help lists every command, and vibe <command> --help says what each one does. The Dashboard is at https://dashboard.vibe.example.com/ . What this release does not have yet is in the release's notes .

This is step 8 of Getting started . vibe versions , vibe go-back and vibe logs show the Versions, serve an earlier one again, and show what the Application printed: see Deploying on The tool's commands.

A deploy sends the project's last commit, so the project must be a Git repository with everything committed: sh git init git add --all git commit -m "The first version" vibe deploy The Application now answers at https://hello.vibe.example.com/ . Open it in your browser: you are its Contributor, so you can open it.

This is step 9 of Getting started . Contributors may change and deploy an Application. It opens for them alone until one of them shares it with people, Groups or everyone. The Dashboard, at https://dashboard.vibe.example.com/ , lists the Applications you contribute to and those shared with you, says what of each will not work for you, and lets a Contributor share one. vibe unshare and vibe contributors are on The tool's commands .

Let others open it. Share it with a person by their email address (they must have signed in to the installation once), with a Group, or with everyone who can sign in: sh vibe share hello --email colleague@example.com vibe share hello --group engineering vibe share hello --everyone
Every command of the tool vibe 0.1.3, as vibe <command> --help prints it. vibe --help lists them all; that list and the exit codes are at the end of this page.

Sign the tool in to an installation, and keep its credential in your own configuration folder Usage: vibe sign-in [OPTIONS] --domain <DOMAIN> Options: --domain <DOMAIN> The installation's domain: the tool speaks HTTPS to api.<domain> --port <PORT> The port of HTTPS (443 when not given) --resolve <RESOLVE> Connect to this IP address (IPv4 or IPv6, written alone) in place of what the system resolves api.<domain> to; nothing else changes: the certificate is checked for api.<domain> --connect <CONNECT> Plain HTTP instead, to an installation on this machine: a loopback address and port, such as 127.0.0.1:8080 or [::1]:8080 --stand-in-user <STAND_IN_USER> Development only, while sign-in is the stand-in: the User to sign in as --stand-in-groups <STAND_IN_GROUPS> Development only: the User's Groups, comma-separated --no-browser Do not open a browser here: show an address to open on any device, and a check code to type there --timeout <TIMEOUT> How long to wait for the sign-in in the browser, in seconds [default: 300] --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help
End the tool's credential at the installation and remove it from this machine Usage: vibe sign-out [OPTIONS] Options: --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help
Who the tool is signed in as: the User, their Groups, the installation Usage: vibe whoami [OPTIONS] Options: --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

Make a new project from the template: an Application that answers one page, ready for npm install and vibe check Usage: vibe new [OPTIONS] <NAME> Arguments: <NAME> The Application's name: a lower-case DNS label (letters, digits and hyphens), which becomes its address Options: --directory <DIRECTORY> Where to make the project: a missing or empty folder. Without it, ./<name> --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

Check whether the project will deploy: its Manifest, its Resources, its migrations and its types, every problem with its fix Usage: vibe check [OPTIONS] Options: --project <PROJECT> The project to check; without it, the current directory --timeout <TIMEOUT> The longest the whole check may take, in seconds (1 to 3600; 300 without it) --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

Generate the next migration from src/db/schema.ts into migrations/, stopping before one that destroys data Usage: vibe generate [OPTIONS] Options: --project <PROJECT> The project; without it, the current directory --name <NAME> The migration's name after its number (0001_<name>): 1 to 100 lower-case letters, digits and _. Without it, drizzle-kit's own --allow-data-loss Generate a migration that destroys data (drops a table, a column or a schema, or changes a type to one that is not wider). Only when the Builder has clearly said that this data may be lost --empty Write an empty migration, for SQL of your own (such as copying values); only when the schema is in step with the migrations --timeout <TIMEOUT> The longest the command may take, in seconds (1 to 3600; 300 without it) --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help
Every registered Resource: its description, your Access level, and whom to ask Usage: vibe resources [OPTIONS] Options: --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

Pull a Resource's structure into the project, as a typed Drizzle definition (resources/<name>/schema.ts) and its link (resources/<name>/index.ts) Usage: vibe pull [OPTIONS] <RESOURCE> Arguments: <RESOURCE> The Resource whose structure to pull Options: --project <PROJECT> The project to write into; without it, the current directory --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

Keep the project running on this machine and serve it to your browser at http://<name>.localhost:7480/, as the test User you choose there; rebuilt when the project changes, until interrupted Usage: vibe dev [OPTIONS] Options: --port <PORT> The port to listen on, on 127.0.0.1 and ::1 only (1 to 65535) [default: 7480] --project <PROJECT> The project; without it, the current directory --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

Run the project on this machine, beside a private Postgres with an empty stand-in of each pulled Resource, and send it one request as a test User of vibe.dev.json (--as builder, --as outsider, ...) Usage: vibe request [OPTIONS] --as <TEST USER> <PATH> Arguments: <PATH> The path to ask for: it begins with /, and may have a query Options: --as <TEST USER> The test User of vibe.dev.json to send the request as (builder, outsider, ...) --method <METHOD> The method: GET without a body, POST with one; any token is taken --header <HEADER> A header, "<name>: <value>"; may be given several times. Host, Content-Length and x-vm-* are the tool's --data <DATA> The body, as text (at most 1 MiB) --data-file <DATA_FILE> The body, the bytes of this file (at most 1 MiB) --project <PROJECT> The project; without it, the current directory --timeout <TIMEOUT> The longest the whole run may take, in seconds (1 to 3600; 300 without it) --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

The project's local runs: what they recorded (operation-log, change-history), and reset, which starts the local databases over Usage: vibe local <COMMAND> Commands: operation-log The local Operation log: the newest entries of the project's local runs, oldest first change-history The local Change history of the own database: the newest changes first, of one table or of all reset Start the local databases over: the own database, the stand-ins, the local Versions and records are made again from nothing, with every migration and the test rows. The project is not touched help Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s) Options: -h, --help Print help

The local Operation log: the newest entries of the project's local runs, oldest first Usage: vibe local operation-log [OPTIONS] Options: --limit <LIMIT> How many entries, the newest (1 to 1000; 100 without it) [default: 100] --project <PROJECT> The project; without it, the current directory --timeout <TIMEOUT> The longest the whole command may take, in seconds (1 to 3600; 300 without it) --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

The local Change history of the own database: the newest changes first, of one table or of all Usage: vibe local change-history [OPTIONS] Options: --table <TABLE> Only the changes of this table: [schema.]table (public without a schema) --limit <LIMIT> How many changes, the newest (1 to 1000; 100 without it) [default: 100] --project <PROJECT> The project; without it, the current directory --timeout <TIMEOUT> The longest the whole command may take, in seconds (1 to 3600; 300 without it) --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

Start the local databases over: the own database, the stand-ins, the local Versions and records are made again from nothing, with every migration and the test rows. The project is not touched Usage: vibe local reset [OPTIONS] Options: --project <PROJECT> The project; without it, the current directory --timeout <TIMEOUT> The longest the whole reset may take, in seconds (1 to 3600; 300 without it) --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

Deploy the project: build it on this machine from its last commit, check it, and send it as the Application's new Version, which goes live at its address Usage: vibe deploy [OPTIONS] Options: --project <PROJECT> The project to deploy; without it, the current directory --allow-data-loss Deploy although a migration this Version adds destroys data while the Application already has a Version. Only when the Builder has clearly said that this data may be lost --timeout <TIMEOUT> The longest the deploy may take on this machine, in seconds (1 to 3600; 300 without it). Sending the Version has its own end --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

The Application's Versions: each one's commit, when and by whom it was deployed, and which one serves Usage: vibe versions [OPTIONS] <APPLICATION> Arguments: <APPLICATION> The Application, by name Options: --limit <LIMIT> How many of the newest Versions to print: 1 to 1000 [default: 100] --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

Serve an earlier Version again, at once: the one before the serving Version, or --to <number>. Migrations are not undone Usage: vibe go-back [OPTIONS] <APPLICATION> Arguments: <APPLICATION> The Application, by name Options: --to <TO> The Version to serve instead: an earlier one than the serving Version. Without it, the one just before --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

What the Application printed and the errors it did not catch, request by request; --follow prints new entries as they come Usage: vibe logs [OPTIONS] <APPLICATION> Arguments: <APPLICATION> The Application, by name Options: --request <REQUEST> Only the entry of this request: a response's x-vm-request-id --after <AFTER> Only the entries after this cursor: the `next` of an earlier run --limit <LIMIT> How many entries, 1 to 1000 (100 without it): the newest, or the oldest after --after --follow Go on printing new entries as they are made, until interrupted --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

The Applications you contribute to and those shared with you: name, description, address, and which is which Usage: vibe applications [OPTIONS] Options: --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

An Application: its address, serving Version, Contributors and whom it is shared with Usage: vibe show [OPTIONS] <APPLICATION> Arguments: <APPLICATION> The Application, by name Options: --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

Share the Application: let people, Groups or everyone signed in open it (--user, --email, --group, --everyone; each as often as needed) Usage: vibe share [OPTIONS] <--user <ID>|--email <ADDRESS>|--group <GROUP>|--everyone> <APPLICATION> Arguments: <APPLICATION> The Application, by name Options: --user <ID> A person, by their user id (vibe whoami shows it) --email <ADDRESS> A person, by their email address: the one who signed in here with it --group <GROUP> A Group, by its name --everyone Everyone who can sign in to the installation --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

Stop sharing the Application with people, Groups or everyone Usage: vibe unshare [OPTIONS] <--user <ID>|--email <ADDRESS>|--group <GROUP>|--everyone> <APPLICATION> Arguments: <APPLICATION> The Application, by name Options: --user <ID> A person, by their user id (vibe whoami shows it) --email <ADDRESS> A person, by their email address: the one who signed in here with it --group <GROUP> A Group, by its name --everyone Everyone who can sign in to the installation --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

Change who maintains the Application: vibe contributors add|remove Usage: vibe contributors <COMMAND> Commands: add Make people or Groups Contributors of the Application: they can open it, deploy it, and change both of its lists remove Take people or Groups off the Application's Contributors (one must be left) help Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s) Options: -h, --help Print help

Make people or Groups Contributors of the Application: they can open it, deploy it, and change both of its lists Usage: vibe contributors add [OPTIONS] <--user <ID>|--email <ADDRESS>|--group <GROUP>> <APPLICATION> Arguments: <APPLICATION> The Application, by name Options: --user <ID> A person, by their user id (vibe whoami shows it) --email <ADDRESS> A person, by their email address: the one who signed in here with it --group <GROUP> A Group, by its name --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

Take people or Groups off the Application's Contributors (one must be left) Usage: vibe contributors remove [OPTIONS] <--user <ID>|--email <ADDRESS>|--group <GROUP>> <APPLICATION> Arguments: <APPLICATION> The Application, by name Options: --user <ID> A person, by their user id (vibe whoami shows it) --email <ADDRESS> A person, by their email address: the one who signed in here with it --group <GROUP> A Group, by its name --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help
vibe serve is the program the image runs; vibe setup is run inside the installation's container: docker compose exec vibe vibe setup .

Serve Applications, each on <name>.<domain>, and the platform's API on api.<domain>. The platform database is named by VIBE_DATABASE_URL, the installation's key is VIBE_SECRET_KEY. To serve HTTPS itself, with no reverse proxy before it, set both VIBE_TLS_CERT_FILE, the PEM file of the certificate for *.<domain> and its chain, and VIBE_TLS_KEY_FILE, the PEM file of its private key (RSA of 2048 to 4096 bits, ECDSA on P-256 or P-384, or Ed25519); they are read again when they change. Without them it serves plain HTTP. Usage: vibe serve [OPTIONS] --domain <DOMAIN> --listen <LISTEN> Options: --domain <DOMAIN> The installation's domain --listen <LISTEN> The address to listen on; port 0 picks a free one --stand-in-sign-in Development only: the caller states the User in x-vm-stand-in-* headers --administrators-group <ADMINISTRATORS_GROUP> With the stand-in only: the Group whose members are Platform administrators. With OIDC the connection names it (vibe admin connect-oidc) --tool-credential-lifetime <TOOL_CREDENTIAL_LIFETIME> How long a tool credential lives from its sign-in, in seconds [default: 2592000] --public-scheme <PUBLIC_SCHEME> How a browser reaches the installation: https (the de

Print the setup credential, good for 24 hours for connecting OIDC once (vibe admin connect-oidc). The platform database is named by VIBE_DATABASE_URL Usage: vibe setup [OPTIONS] Options: --json Print exactly one JSON object on standard output -h, --help Print help

Connect OIDC, with the setup credential or as a Platform administrator signed in. With the setup credential in VIBE_SETUP_CREDENTIAL, --domain says where the installation is: over HTTPS, with --port and --resolve as for vibe sign-in, or over plain HTTP on this machine with --connect. Without it, the command goes to the installation the tool is signed in to. The client secret is read from VIBE_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET. Usage: vibe admin connect-oidc [OPTIONS] --issuer <ISSUER> --client-id <CLIENT_ID> --administrators-group <ADMINISTRATORS_GROUP> Options: --domain <DOMAIN> With the setup credential: the installation's domain --port <PORT> The port of HTTPS (443 when not given) --resolve <RESOLVE> Connect to this IP address (IPv4 or IPv6, written alone) in place of what the system resolves api.<domain> to; nothing else changes: the certificate is checked for api.<domain> --connect <CONNECT> Plain HTTP instead, to an installation on this machine: a loopback address and port, such as 127.0.0.1:8080 or [::1]:8080 --issuer <ISSUER> The identity provider's issuer, https://... (http:// only on a loopback host) --client-id <CLIENT_ID> The platform's client id at the identity provider --administrat

An Application is written with the SDK, @vm/sdk . These are its types, sdk/index.d.ts , as they are in the repository, cut into their parts. A project made by vibe new has them already; its AGENTS.md tells you and your coding agent how to work in it. The words are those of the Glossary : a Manifest, a Resource and its Access level, the Trusted context, the Change history.

ts // @vm/sdk: what an Application is written with (blackbox/CONTRACT.md, "The SDK"). // // manifest.ts: export default defineManifest({ name, description, resources }) // src/index.ts: export default defineApp(manifest, { fetch(request, ctx) { ... } }) // // ctx.user().db("devops") a shared database declared in manifest.ts, as the User // ctx.user().ownDb() the Application's own database, as the User // ctx.app().ownDb() the Application's own database, as the Application // // A handle is a Drizzle database typed with that database's structure: a // shared one from resources/<name>/ (linked by its generated index.ts), the // own one from src/db/schema.ts (tsconfig "paths": "@vm/own-structure"). // The types guide; the platform decides. Every operation is decided by the // host from the request in flight, and the database role is the boundary. import type { PgTable, PgTransactionConfig } from "drizzle-orm/pg-core"; import type { PgRemoteDatabase } from "drizzle-orm/pg-proxy"; import type * as OwnStructureModule from "@vm/own-structure"; declare const contextBrand: unique symbol;

ts /** An Access level a Manifest declares. (`structure` is for building only.) */ export type DeclaredAccess = "read" | "write"; /** A shared database the Application uses. */ export interface ResourceDeclaration { readonly kind: "postgres"; readonly access: DeclaredAccess; } export interface Manifest { /** The Application's name: a lower-case DNS label, as the platform's API takes it. */ readonly name: string; /** One sentence saying what the Application does, and for whom. */ readonly description: string; /** Every shared database the Application uses, by its Resource name. */ readonly resources: { readonly [name: string]: ResourceDeclaration }; } /** Write the argument as a plain literal: the platform reads manifest.ts without running it. */ export declare function defineManifest<const M extends Manifest>(manifest: M): M;

This takes you from a Linux machine with Docker to a person signed in. The platform is one container image, vibe , started by compose.yaml beside a Postgres 18 and a reverse proxy that terminates TLS. You need: a machine with Docker Engine 25.0 or later and its Compose plugin 2.24.1 or later: docker version --format '{{.Server.Version}}' prints the Engine's version, docker compose version the plugin's. That minimum is read from Docker's notes and was not run; the install tests ran with Engine 28.0.4 and Compose 2.38.2, and with Engine 29.2.1 and Compose 5.0.2 (see Why these versions of Docker , at the end); a domain for the installation, here vibe.example.com , whose names all reach the machine: Applications are at <name>.vibe.example.com , the platform's API at api.vibe.example.com , sign-in at auth.vibe.example.com , the Dashboard at dashboard.vibe.example.com (a DNS record for *.vibe.example.com ); a certificate for *.vibe.example.com and its private key, in PEM; an OIDC identity provider at which you can register a client; the tool vibe on the computer you connect OIDC from. Replace vibe.example.com with your domain in every command below.

Make a folder for the installation and put the files of this folder in it: compose.yaml , compose.own-proxy.yaml , compose.own-tls.yaml , compose.own-postgres.yaml and .env.example , and the two folders ca/ and certs/ . sh mkdir -p /opt/vibe/ca /opt/vibe/certs cd /opt/vibe Every command below is run in this folder.

compose.yaml reads its values from .env beside it. .env.example lists every value and what it is for. Three are required: the domain, the installation's key and the bundled Postgres's password. sh cp .env.example .env chmod 600 .env sed -i "s|^VIBE_DOMAIN=.*|VIBE_DOMAIN=vibe.example.com|" .env sed -i "s|^VIBE_SECRET_KEY=.*|VIBE_SECRET_KEY=$(openssl rand -base64 32)|" .env sed -i "s|^POSTGRES_PASSWORD=.*|POSTGRES_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 24)|" .env VIBE_SECRET_KEY is the installation's key ( openssl rand -base64 32 ). It seals the OIDC connection and the sessions in the platform database. Keep .env as long as you keep the data: with another key, OIDC has to be connected again. POSTGRES_PASSWORD is the password of the role vibe in the bundled Postgres ( openssl rand -hex 24 ). Without VIBE_DOMAIN or VIBE_SECRET_KEY , docker compose refuses to start and names the value. Without POSTGRES_PASSWORD , or with it empty, the bundled Postgres does not start: docker compose up -d ends with an error ( dependency failed to start: container ... is unhealthy ), vibe is not started, docker compose ps shows postgres restarting, and docker compose logs postgres names POSTGRES_PASSWORD . If the v

Put your certificate for *.vibe.example.com , followed by its intermediate certificates, in certs/fullchain.pem , and its private key in certs/privkey.pem . The proxy runs as the user 65532 , not as root; make the key readable by that user and nobody else: sh cp /path/to/fullchain.pem certs/fullchain.pem cp /path/to/privkey.pem certs/privkey.pem chmod 644 certs/fullchain.pem sudo chown 65532 certs/privkey.pem sudo chmod 600 certs/privkey.pem The proxy speaks TLS 1.2 and 1.3 with this certificate and passes every request on to the platform with its Host unchanged. It sets no limit of its own on a request's size or time: the platform's own apply (a request body of at most 16 MiB). When the proxy cannot read the key, it does not start: docker compose ps shows it restarting, and docker compose logs proxy says open /etc/caddy/certs/privkey.pem: permission denied . Give the key to the user 65532 as above and run docker compose restart proxy . With no proxy at all, the program can serve this certificate itself: see The program serves TLS itself .

sh docker compose up -d This starts three containers: postgres (the bundled Postgres 18, its data in the volume postgres-data , published nowhere), vibe (the program, published nowhere) and proxy (published on VIBE_BIND:VIBE_HTTPS_PORT ). The first start of Postgres makes the role vibe and the platform database vibe ; vibe starts once that first start has finished and Postgres takes connections ( docker compose ps shows postgres as healthy ). Only HTTPS is served, on the published port alone. Nothing listens for plain http:// (port 80 is not published) and nothing redirects it to https:// ; a plain HTTP request sent to the published port is refused with 400 . If you want http:// addresses to be redirected, do it in a proxy of your own (see "Your own reverse proxy"). Check that it answers: sh docker compose ps curl https://api.vibe.example.com/v1/installation The answer is {"domain":"vibe.example.com","sign_in":"none","sign_in_address":null} : no sign-in is connected yet. The program's log is the vibe container's: docker compose logs vibe .

sh docker compose exec vibe vibe setup This prints the setup credential ( vmsc_... ) once, on your terminal and in no log. It is good for 24 hours and for one thing: connecting OIDC, once. Running it again ends the earlier one.

h: If the first start was interrupted
t: The first start of the bundled Postgres makes its data folder, then the role vibe , the platform database and the rest, and leaves a mark when it has finished. If the container was stopped or killed in between (the machine went down, docker compose down during the first up ), Postgres starts again on what was made so far and skips the rest. It is then never healthy: docker compose ps shows postgres as health: starting for two minutes and as unhealthy after that, vibe is not started, and docker compose up -d ends with dependency failed to start: container ... is unhealthy . The health check says why: sh docker compose ps docker inspect --format '{{json .State.Health.Log}}' $(docker compose ps --quiet postgres) Its output says the first start of this Postgres did not finish . Meanwhile you can look inside as the superuser: docker compose exec postgres psql -U postgres . Nothing is in it yet, since vibe never started on it: remove it and start again. sh docker compose down --volumes docker compose up -d

The platform connects as the role vibe , never as a superuser. The superuser postgres cannot connect over the network at all, whatever password is given; you reach it inside the container: sh docker compose exec postgres psql -U postgres CONNECT on the databases postgres and template1 is taken from PUBLIC at its first start.

h: 6. Register the platform at the identity provider
t: At your identity provider, register a client for the platform (an OpenID Connect client with a client secret, the authorization code flow): the redirect address: https://auth.vibe.example.com/callback ; with VIBE_HTTPS_PORT other than 443, the port is in it: https://auth.vibe.example.com:8443/callback ; the scopes: openid profile email offline_access (another list can be given to vibe admin connect-oidc with --scopes ); a refresh token for the platform: the provider must allow offline_access for this client and for every person who signs in, or the sign-in fails. In Keycloak, for example, a person needs its role offline_access : people made in its console have it by default, people made by a realm import may not, and for them the sign-in ended on the platform's page with "The company's sign-in refused the code it gave" and the log record identity-provider-refused with the error not_allowed ; the person's Groups in the ID token, in the claim groups (another claim can be given with --groups-claim ); the ID token signed with RS256 or ES256 . Note the issuer, the client id and the client secret, and choose the Group whose members are Platform administrators.

With the tool, from any computer that reaches the installation over HTTPS: sh read -rs VIBE_SETUP_CREDENTIAL && export VIBE_SETUP_CREDENTIAL read -rs VIBE_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET && export VIBE_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET vibe admin connect-oidc --domain vibe.example.com \ --issuer https://idp.example.com \ --client-id vibe \ --administrators-group vibe-administrators The two read lines ask for the setup credential and the client secret without showing them or keeping them in the shell's history. With VIBE_HTTPS_PORT other than 443, add --port <the port> ; while the domain is not in DNS yet, --resolve <the machine's address> connects there in its place. The platform asks the identity provider for its configuration before it takes the connection; when it cannot use it, the command says why and nothing is changed. When it is taken, curl https://api.vibe.example.com/v1/installation says "sign_in":"oidc" .

In a browser, open https://dashboard.vibe.example.com/ : it sends you to the identity provider and back, signed in. The tool signs in through the browser: sh vibe sign-in --domain vibe.example.com vibe whoami An Application can be shared with someone by their email address once that person has signed in here once; before that the platform refuses ( unknown-email , and the Dashboard says nobody who signed in here has that email address).

The platform's page says in one sentence what failed, and the program's log has the record of it ( docker compose logs vibe ): {"event":"identity-provider-refused","status",...,"error",...} : the identity provider refused the platform's call to its token endpoint; error is the provider's own error code (never its description), for example not_allowed when it does not allow offline_access (step 6); {"event":"identity-provider-unanswered","call",...,"problem",...} : a call to the provider brought no answer the platform could use; call is configuration , keys or token , problem says what was wrong ( unreachable , timed-out , too-large , status , not-json , no-id-token , another-issuer , lacks-endpoint , unreadable-keys ), with the answer's status when it had one. The person's browser and the tool's computer must trust the installation's certificate: one from a public authority, or the company's own authority installed on them (for the tool, VIBE_CA_FILE : see Your company's own certificate authority ).

When your identity provider's certificate is issued by your company's own certificate authority, the platform has to trust it. Put the authority's certificate (PEM, one or more certificates, at most 1 MiB) in ca/ and name it as the container sees it: sh cp /path/to/company-ca.pem ca/company-ca.pem chmod 644 ca/company-ca.pem echo "VIBE_CA_FILE=/etc/vibe/ca/company-ca.pem" >> .env docker compose up -d It is trusted beside the public authorities built into the program, read when the program starts. The tool takes the same variable: when the installation's own certificate is issued by such an authority, set VIBE_CA_FILE=/path/to/company-ca.pem in the tool's environment on each computer that uses it.

The platform is served over HTTPS only, with a certificate for *.vibe.example.com . There are three ways to end TLS: The Compose file's reverse proxy , as compose.yaml starts it: put the certificate in certs/ ( 3. The certificate ) and start with docker compose up -d . Your own reverse proxy , with compose.own-proxy.yaml : below. The program itself , with compose.own-tls.yaml : below.

Instead of the proxy of compose.yaml : sh docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.own-proxy.yaml up -d There is no proxy container then, and the program's own port is published, plain HTTP, at VIBE_HTTP_BIND:VIBE_HTTP_PORT ( 127.0.0.1:8080 without them), for your proxy only. Your proxy terminates TLS for *.vibe.example.com and must pass Host on unchanged. Set VIBE_HTTPS_PORT to the port your proxy is reached at when it is not 443: the addresses the platform writes come from it, never from a header of the request.

Instead of the proxy of compose.yaml , for an installation that wants no proxy before the program: vibe itself ends TLS with the certificate and key of certs/ (step 3) and is published at VIBE_BIND:VIBE_HTTPS_PORT ( 127.0.0.1:443 without them). sh docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.own-tls.yaml up -d There is no proxy container then. vibe reads certs/fullchain.pem (your certificate for *.vibe.example.com first, its intermediate certificates after it, at most ten certificates) and certs/privkey.pem (its key, not encrypted: PRIVATE KEY , RSA PRIVATE KEY or EC PRIVATE KEY ; an RSA key of 2048 to 4096 bits, an ECDSA key on P-256 or P-384, or an Ed25519 key, the kinds the program takes), mounted read-only at /etc/vibe/certs . It runs as the image's user 65532 , not as root, so the key must be readable by that user: sh sudo chown 65532 certs/privkey.pem sudo chmod 600 certs/privkey.pem It serves HTTPS only on that port (TLS 1.2 and 1.3, HTTP/1.1); a plain HTTP request to it gets no answer and its connection is closed. Everything the platform writes is the same as behind the proxy: the addresses come from VIBE_HTTPS_PORT . The program checks the two files when it starts, and does n

Instead of the bundled one: your Postgres 18 (no other major version is taken; the vibe container's log says so and nothing is written). Do two things on it first, as its superuser: Make a role for the platform that may create databases and roles and is not a superuser, and the platform database owned by it: sql CREATE ROLE vibe LOGIN CREATEDB CREATEROLE PASSWORD '<a password>'; CREATE DATABASE vibe OWNER vibe; Take CONNECT on the databases postgres and template1 from PUBLIC . Every role may connect to them otherwise, the roles the platform makes for Applications' own databases included, and the platform, which is no superuser, cannot take it away itself: sql REVOKE CONNECT ON DATABASE postgres FROM PUBLIC; REVOKE CONNECT ON DATABASE template1 FROM PUBLIC; Then set its address in .env and start with the second file: sh echo "VIBE_DATABASE_URL=postgres://vibe:<the password>@db.example.com:5432/vibe" >> .env docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.own-postgres.yaml up -d There is no postgres container and no volume then, and POSTGRES_PASSWORD is not needed. The two other files can be given together: docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.own-proxy.yaml -f compose.own-postgres.ya

Set the newer image in .env and start again: sh sed -i "s|^#\?VIBE_IMAGE=.*|VIBE_IMAGE=ghcr.io/irvingouj/vibe:<the newer version>|" .env docker compose pull && docker compose up -d The platform database, every Application's own database, the OIDC connection and the sessions are kept: the data is the volume's, the key is the .env 's.

sh docker compose down stops and removes the containers and keeps the data; docker compose up -d brings it back as it was. Only sh docker compose down --volumes removes the bundled Postgres's data, every Application's included, for good.

vibe runs with a read-only root filesystem, every capability dropped, no-new-privileges , as the image's user 65532 (not root), with no writable volume and no tmpfs; its one mount is ca/ , read-only, at /etc/vibe/ca (with compose.own-tls.yaml , certs/ too, read-only, at /etc/vibe/certs ). The installation's key and the database's address are in its environment, in no command line. vibe may open 65,536 files ( ulimits: nofile , soft and hard), whatever the Docker daemon's default, so that it never runs out of files before its own bound of 1,024 connections at once; started elsewhere, the program raises its own soft limit towards the hard one and logs open-files-limit-low when even the hard limit is below 4,096. postgres runs as its image's user 999 and proxy as 65532 , neither as root, each with every capability dropped and no-new-privileges . Not possible: a read-only root filesystem for postgres and proxy . Each takes a file of compose.yaml 's configs (Postgres's first-start script, the proxy's configuration), and Compose cannot place such a file into a read-only container.

The install tests ran with two pairs of versions: Docker Engine 28.0.4 with Compose 2.38.2 (GitHub's hosted runner, in the release workflow), and Docker Engine 29.2.1 with Compose 5.0.2 (the machine of the install gate). The minimum this document gives, Engine 25.0 and Compose 2.24.1, was not run: it is read from Docker's notes. The Compose files use three things that older versions do not have, each according to Docker's own notes: a config written in the file itself ( configs: ... content: ), for the Postgres first-start script and the proxy's configuration: Compose 2.23.1 ( Compose file reference, configs : " content : The content is created with the inlined value. Introduced in Docker Compose version 2.23.1"); the health check's start_interval , so that a fresh install is seen healthy within seconds: Docker Engine 25.0.0 ( Engine 25.0 release notes , "Add an additional interval to be used by healthchecks during the container start period") and Compose 2.24.0, whose release notes list "Add support for start_interval", with the check of the Engine's version it needs fixed in 2.24.1 ("fix engine version require to use healthcheck.start_interval"); !reset , by which compose.own-pro

The fourth release of the platform, still a minimal one, to try it for real. It holds the platform's image, the Compose files that install it, and the tool vibe for Linux and macOS. Getting started takes you from nothing to an Application open in your browser. This release is not for untrusted Applications or real company data. Use it with Applications you wrote yourself and with data you can lose. It stays so until the work on three things is done: the credentials of shared databases (kept encrypted, revoked, replaced), the limits on what one request of an Application may use, and the hardening of the runtime that runs Applications.

The pages say each thing once. The Dashboard's list no longer repeats the Contributors and every Resource on each Application; a refusal, the sign-out page and the pages for an address that does not exist no longer say under their title what the title said. Buttons are short ("Open", "Share") and keep the Application's name for a screen reader. Marks before words. A state is a mark with a colour and a shape: a lock for an Application that is not shared with you, a check, a cross, a warning. A person, a Group and everyone each have their mark where an Application's sharing is listed. A Resource's standing is a mark in a table of what the Application needs and what you hold. Every mark has a name a screen reader says. The list first, the rest one step away. An Application in the Dashboard's list shows its name, its description, "Open" and at most one mark when a part of it will not work for you ("Missing access", "Not set up", "Access unknown"). Its Contributors, its Resources and whom to ask, its Version and its address are on its own page, which its name leads to. Smaller things. A page of the sign-in address says which installation it is. The page of test Users of vibe dev names i

Installing. One image and one Compose file start the platform beside a bundled Postgres 18 and a reverse proxy that terminates TLS with your wildcard certificate. You can use your own reverse proxy or your own Postgres 18 instead, or have the program serve TLS itself. Upgrading keeps every database, the OIDC connection and the sessions. Signing in. People sign in with your company's identity provider (OIDC). Their Groups come from it. Platform administrators are the members of one Group you name. The tool signs in through the browser. Making an Application. vibe new makes a project from the template. vibe check says whether it will deploy, with each problem and its fix. vibe generate writes the next migration of the Application's own database, and stops before a migration that destroys data. Shared databases. A Builder lists the Resources ( vibe resources ) and pulls one's structure into the project as a typed definition ( vibe pull ). An Application reads and writes a Resource only as its Grants allow, as the person who uses it. Running it on your computer. vibe dev serves the Application to your browser as a test User you choose, with test rows, beside a private Postgres. vibe re

These are not in this release. Each is planned. Shared databases' credentials are kept in the platform database without encryption. Registering a Resource is done through the platform's API only: the tool has no command for it, nor for listing, changing or revoking Grants. There are no limits per request yet: one Application can use as much CPU time, memory and time as it likes, and so slow down the others. The runtime that runs Applications is not yet closed against every way an Application could stop the whole program. An Application cannot call services outside the platform ( fetch to the internet). An Application cannot serve static files: its pages are strings in its code. An Application cannot be deleted. An Application's source is not kept on the platform: it stays in your own Git repository. Platform administrators cannot yet see every Application, disable one, or read the Operation log with the tool. There is no report of Applications built against an older structure of a shared database that has changed. Coding agents use the tool's commands; there is no MCP interface yet. The tool is not on npm, and there is no Windows build. The SDK is not on npm either. After signing i

The image is for linux/amd64 only. There is no image for linux/arm64 . The tool is built for two targets: x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu : Linux on x86-64 with glibc 2.35 or later (Ubuntu 22.04, Debian 12 and later). It was built on Ubuntu 22.04. aarch64-apple-darwin : macOS on Apple silicon. It is not signed by a developer and not notarised by Apple: downloaded with a browser, macOS holds it back until you remove its quarantine mark ( xattr -d com.apple.quarantine vibe ). What was tried. The release workflow ran no test of the program for this release: since 2026-11-21 it checks the versions, builds the image and the tool, tries the packed tool as below, and publishes; the whole set of tests (the gate) and the install tests come back to it when the product is in use. Before the tag, on a Linux machine of 12 cores: the release check; the format and lint checks of every crate; the program's own tests; and, each alone, the test files of the pages and of the release's files (the Dashboard's, the sharing's, the sign-in's and the local run's pages in a real Firefox, the walk that measures the pages in light and in dark, release_* ). The whole gate last ran on the tree of 0.1.2, before the pag

SHA256SUMS : the SHA-256 of each file. Check your downloads with sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS (Linux) or shasum -a 256 --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS (macOS). The image: ghcr.io/irvingouj/vibe:0.1.3 .
An open-source, self-hosted platform on which an enterprise's employees and their AI coding agents build, deploy and run internal applications against shared, IT-governed infrastructure.

Application : A stateless program, deployed by a Builder, that answers web requests and reaches enterprise infrastructure only through the SDK. It follows the Cloudflare Workers execution model without being Cloudflare-compatible. Avoid : Worker (reserved for future background compute), service, project Manifest : The TypeScript value in an Application's project that names the Application and lists the Resources it uses. Deploy turns it into the Application's Declared access. Avoid : Config, bindings file, wrangler file Version : One deploy of an Application, kept unchanged: its bundled code, its Declared access and the Git commit it was built from. An Application serves exactly one Version at a time, and going back means serving the previous one. Avoid : Release, build, revision, deployment (for the thing; deploy is the act) Dashboard : The page every employee signs in to, listing the Applications they can contribute to and the Applications shared with them. The same list is available to their agent. Avoid : Portal, console (IT's admin surface), app store Integration : Separately trusted code that exposes a few narrow business functions and reaches Resources as itself. Application

Grant : A Platform administrator's statement that a Group may reach a Resource at a given access level. It names a Group, never a single User, and covers the whole Resource. It holds in every Application, and it also decides who may build against the Resource. Avoid : Permission, ACL, role Access level : How much of a Resource a Grant opens. For a database there are three, each including the one before: structure (pull its table structure, no rows), read, and write. Avoid : Role, permission set, scope Group : A set of Users defined in the enterprise directory and reported by the identity provider. The platform does not define its own. Grants are given to Groups. Avoid : Role, team, access list Declared access : The list, taken from an Application's Manifest at deploy and fixed for that Version, of the Resources it uses and at what access level. Nothing outside it is reachable. Avoid : Binding, scope, app permission Autonomous grant : A Grant that lets code reach a Resource as itself, whatever the User it is serving may access. Only an Integration can hold one on a shared Resource; an Application acts as itself only in its own database. Avoid : Service account, elevated access, bypa

Operation log : The platform's record of every operation on a Resource: who, through which Application, what statement, how many rows, and whether it succeeded. It contains none of the Resource's data. Avoid : Audit trail (ambiguous between the two layers), access log Change history : The record of each row that was changed in an Application's own database: old value, new value, who and through which Application. The platform keeps it in the platform database, out of reach of the database a Contributor's migrations run in (ADR 0017). Readable, through the Application, by whoever may use the Application. Avoid : Audit log, versioning, revision table

Platform administrator : A member of the one directory Group named when the platform is installed. They register Resources, write Grants, see every Application and can disable any of them. The platform keeps no administrator accounts of its own. Avoid : Superuser, root, IT (when this specific role is meant) Builder : An employee who creates and deploys an Application, normally by directing a Coding agent. Any signed-in employee may create one. Avoid : Developer, author, employee (when the building role is meant) Contributor : A person or Group allowed to change and deploy a given Application. An Application has no owner: it belongs to the company, and what is controlled is who may contribute to it. Avoid : Owner, maintainer, author User : An employee who signs in to a deployed Application and uses it. Avoid : End user, customer, employee (when the using role is meant) Coding agent : An AI tool that writes Application code at a Builder's direction. Avoid : AI, bot, agent (unqualified)
